# Generate Images and Video with ComfyUI

> FLUX.2 image and LTX-2 video workflows you run locally with full creative control

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Instructions](#instructions)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

---

## Overview

## Basic idea

Visual generative AI lets you create photorealistic images and coherent video clips from text (and image) prompts — with creative control that cloud generators often limit. Running these workflows **locally on your hardware platform** keeps assets under your control, avoids per-token cloud costs, and shortens the iteration loop that real creative projects need.

**ComfyUI** is an open-source, node-based app for advanced image and video generation. You install it, load templates for models such as **FLUX.2** and **LTX-2**, download model weights on demand, and build or save workflows as reusable graphs.

- **Local creative control** — refine prompts and graphs at your own pace without cloud round-trips
- **Template-first start** — Getting Started and All Templates paths cover text-to-image and image-to-video
- **VRAM-aware model choices** — pick precision and settings that fit your GPU memory

## What you'll accomplish

You'll install ComfyUI on your hardware platform, run a starter text-to-image workflow, generate images with **FLUX.2-Dev**, generate video with **LTX-2**, and optionally combine both into one custom workflow.

## What to know before starting

**Required:**

- Comfort installing and launching desktop applications on your hardware platform
- Enough free disk space for large model weight downloads (tens of GB per model)

**Optional:**

- Familiarity with generative AI prompting (subject, framing, style, mood)
- Experience with node-based tools or graph editors

## Supported hardware platforms

Use the matrix below to confirm your hardware platform, recommended default local settings, and whether multi-node applies.

| Hardware platform | OS | Memory | Recommended default local settings | Multi-node capable hardware |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **GeForce RTX** | Windows (ComfyUI desktop / portable); Linux paths noted for outputs | Dedicated VRAM (size varies by GPU) | ComfyUI from [comfy.org](https://comfy.org) · starter text-to-image template · FLUX.2-Dev · LTX-2 Image to Video · prefer lower-precision weights that fit your VRAM | — |
| **RTX PRO** | Windows (ComfyUI desktop / portable); Linux paths noted for outputs | Dedicated VRAM (size varies by GPU) | ComfyUI from [comfy.org](https://comfy.org) · starter text-to-image template · FLUX.2-Dev · LTX-2 Image to Video · prefer lower-precision weights that fit your VRAM | — |

## Prerequisites

**Hardware requirements**

- Supported hardware platform — see Supported hardware platforms matrix above
- Enough GPU memory for the model and resolution you choose (frontier video models need more VRAM as resolution, length, and steps increase)
- Enough storage for ComfyUI plus model weights (individual models can exceed 30 GB)

**Software requirements**

- Network access to download ComfyUI and model weights (for example from Hugging Face via ComfyUI’s download dialog)
- A web browser (ComfyUI UI and optional image preview)
- For the Windows install path in **Instructions**: use the ComfyUI download from [comfy.org](https://comfy.org)

## Time & risk

- **Estimated time:** 13 MIN for install and first starter image; longer on first run of FLUX.2 or LTX-2 while model weights download
- **Risk level:** Low to Medium
  - Large model downloads can fail on unstable networks
  - High resolution, frame count, or step counts can exhaust GPU memory or slow generation sharply
- **Rollback:** Quit ComfyUI and uninstall or delete the ComfyUI install folder; delete downloaded model weights and saved workflows you no longer need
- **Last Updated:** 08/03/2026
  - Local ComfyUI workflow for FLUX.2 image and LTX-2 video generation on supported hardware platforms

## Instructions

## Step 1. Install and launch ComfyUI

Visit [comfy.org](https://comfy.org) to download and install ComfyUI for Windows, then launch ComfyUI on your hardware platform.

> [!NOTE]
> This playbook follows the desktop / portable ComfyUI path from [comfy.org](https://comfy.org). It does **not** invent host Python, Docker, or shell install commands. For a Linux host/container ComfyUI path on other hardware platforms, see [Generate Images and Videos with ComfyUI](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/comfyui).

## Step 2. Create a first image with the starter template

1. Click **Templates**, then **Getting Started**, and choose **1.1 Starter - Text to Image**.
2. Connect the model node to the **Save Image** node so the graph forms a complete pipeline.
3. Press the blue **Run** button and watch the green node highlights as your hardware platform generates the first image.

Change the prompt and run again to iterate.

## Step 3. Generate images with FLUX.2-Dev

1. Open **Templates** → **All Templates** and search for **FLUX.2 Dev Text to Image**.
2. Select the template. ComfyUI loads the connected nodes (the workflow).
3. When prompted, download the model weights. Weight files (`.safetensors`) save into the correct ComfyUI folders automatically. FLUX.2 can exceed 30 GB depending on the version — allow time and disk space.
4. Save the workflow: open the top-left hamburger menu and choose **Save**. Press **W** to show or hide the Workflows list.

If you close the download dialog before weights finish:

1. Press **W** to open **Workflows**
2. Select the workflow again so ComfyUI reloads it and re-prompts for any missing weights

**Prompt tips for FLUX.2-Dev**

- Start with clear subject, setting, style, and mood — for example: “Cinematic closeup of a vintage race car in the rain, neon reflections on wet asphalt, high contrast, 35mm photography.” Short-to-medium prompts are usually easier to control than long storylike prompts when learning.
- Add constraints for framing (“wide shot” / “portrait”), detail (“high detail, sharp focus”), and realism (“photorealistic” / “stylized illustration”).
- If results feel busy, remove adjectives instead of adding more.
- Avoid negative prompting — describe what you want.

Learn more in the [Black Forest Labs FLUX.2 prompting guide](https://docs.bfl.ai/guides/prompting_guide_flux2).

**Save locations**

Right-click the **Save Image** node to open the image in a browser or save it elsewhere. Default ComfyUI output folders are typically:

- Windows (standalone / portable): under the ComfyUI install (for example an `output` folder beside the app)
- Windows (desktop application): under the AppData directory
- Linux: under the ComfyUI install location

## Step 4. Generate video with LTX-2

Use the **LTX-2 Image to Video** template. Lightricks’ LTX-2 is an audio-video model for controllable, storyboard-style generation in ComfyUI. Unlike the starter and FLUX.2 text-to-image templates, this workflow combines an **image** and a **text prompt**.

1. Download the **LTX-2 Image to Video** template and its model weights when prompted.
2. Use an image from your FLUX.2-Dev run (or another still) as the image input.
3. Write the prompt like a short shot description, not a full movie script.

A walkthrough video is available here: [LTX-2 in ComfyUI](https://youtu.be/ifxOXmL351I?si=xf2_j01BAQlUhfhY0).

**Prompt tips for LTX-2**

Write a single flowing paragraph in the present tense, or a simple script-style format with scene headings, action, character names, and dialogue. Aim for four to six sentences that:

- Establish shot and scene (wide / medium / closeup, lighting, color, textures, atmosphere)
- Describe action as a clear sequence, with visible character traits, body language, and camera moves
- Add audio (ambient sound, music, dialogue in quotation marks)

Match detail to shot scale — closeups need more precise character and texture detail than wide shots. Useful prompt ingredients include camera movement language, shot type, pacing, atmosphere, style, lighting, emotion, and voice/audio.

**VRAM and quality**

LTX-2 uses significant VRAM. Memory use rises with resolution, frame rate, length, and steps. ComfyUI can stream weights to system memory when GPU memory runs short — that can keep a run going at the cost of speed. Constrain resolution, length, and steps for reasonable generation times on your hardware platform.

Learn more in the [Quick Start Guide for LTX-2 In ComfyUI](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/rtx-ai-video-generation-guide/).

## Step 5. Combine FLUX.2-Dev and LTX-2 in one workflow (optional)

To avoid hopping between workflows when turning a still into video:

1. Open your saved **FLUX.2-Dev Text to Image** workflow.
2. Ctrl+left-click the FLUX.2-Dev Text to Image node to copy it.
3. In the **LTX-2 Image to Video** workflow, paste with Ctrl+V.
4. Drag from the FLUX.2-Dev node **IMAGE** output to the **Resize Image/Mask** input so a blue connector appears.
5. Save under a new name, then prompt for image and video in one graph.

## Step 6. Cleanup (optional)

Cleanup is optional rollback — not required to finish the playbook.

1. Quit ComfyUI
2. Delete saved workflows you no longer need from the Workflows list or on disk
3. Remove downloaded model weights you do not want to keep (large `.safetensors` files under your ComfyUI model folders)
4. Uninstall or delete the ComfyUI application folder if you want a full rollback

## Step 7. Next steps

1. Explore additional ComfyUI templates for advanced image and video models
2. Follow the [NVIDIA Blueprint for 3D-guided generative AI](https://github.com/NVIDIA-AI-Blueprints/3d-guided-genai-rtx) for 3D-guided image and video pipelines
3. Share work and get help in the [Stable Diffusion subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/StableDiffusion/) and [ComfyUI Discord](https://discord.com/invite/comfyorg)
4. For Linux host/container ComfyUI setups on other supported hardware catalogs, see [Generate Images and Videos with ComfyUI](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/comfyui)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| ComfyUI will not install or launch from comfy.org | Incomplete download, blocked installer, or unsupported OS for this desktop path | Re-download from [comfy.org](https://comfy.org), confirm you are on a supported Windows install path for this playbook, and retry launch |
| Model weight download dialog closed early / workflow fails on missing weights | Required `.safetensors` files were not finished downloading | Press **W**, reopen the workflow, and complete the download prompts; confirm enough free disk space (FLUX.2 can exceed 30 GB) |
| Out of memory or very slow LTX-2 / FLUX.2 runs | Resolution, length, frame rate, steps, or precision exceed available GPU memory | Lower resolution, frame count, length, or steps; choose lower-precision weights that fit your VRAM; close other GPU apps; allow weight streaming to system memory only if you accept slower runs |
| Generated image or video quality is poor or chaotic | Prompt is too long, contradictory, or underspecified | Shorten the prompt; state subject, framing, style, and mood clearly; for LTX-2 use a short shot description with camera and audio cues (see **Instructions**) |
| Cannot find saved images on disk | Looking outside ComfyUI’s default output folders | Check the install `output` folder (portable), AppData paths (Windows desktop app), or the ComfyUI install location (Linux); or right-click **Save Image** to open/save explicitly |
| Nodes will not connect / Run does nothing | Graph is incomplete (model not linked to Save Image or required inputs missing) | Re-open the template, connect required outputs to inputs until the pipeline is complete, then press **Run** |

> [!NOTE]
> On discrete-GPU hardware platforms, GPU memory is separate from system RAM. CUDA out-of-memory or stalled generation usually means the workload exceeds VRAM: reduce resolution, length, steps, or model precision; enable ComfyUI weight streaming only if you accept slower performance; close other GPU applications.

For latest known issues, see the documentation linked under **Resources** for your hardware platform.

# Serve LLMs with vLLM Across DGX Sparks

> Guided and configurable model serving across DGX Spark clusters

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Intermediate](#intermediate)
  - [Step 1. Connect and set up the two Sparks](#step-1-connect-and-set-up-the-two-sparks)
  - [Step 2. Set up the launcher on the head Spark](#step-2-set-up-the-launcher-on-the-head-spark)
  - [Step 3. Choose a model and save its recipe](#step-3-choose-a-model-and-save-its-recipe)
  - [Step 4. Download the image and launch the model](#step-4-download-the-image-and-launch-the-model)
  - [Step 5. Check the API on the head Spark](#step-5-check-the-api-on-the-head-spark)
  - [Step 6. Reach the model from your laptop](#step-6-reach-the-model-from-your-laptop)
  - [Step 7. Stop and restart the model](#step-7-stop-and-restart-the-model)
- [Advanced](#advanced)
  - [Step 1. Choose a model and prepare the cluster](#step-1-choose-a-model-and-prepare-the-cluster)
  - [Step 2. Read the distributed and memory settings](#step-2-read-the-distributed-and-memory-settings)
  - [Step 3. Start a container on each Spark](#step-3-start-a-container-on-each-spark)
  - [Step 4. Run the model on the head and worker](#step-4-run-the-model-on-the-head-and-worker)
  - [Step 5. Test the API and tool calling](#step-5-test-the-api-and-tool-calling)
  - [Step 6. Connect a client and tune the workload](#step-6-connect-a-client-and-tune-the-workload)
  - [Step 7. Stop or save the service](#step-7-stop-or-save-the-service)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

---

## Overview

## Basic idea

If you want to run a workload or a model that won't fit on a single DGX Spark, you can connect two or more Sparks into a cluster and distribute the workload or model across the devices.

However, this takes a bit of set up and experience. 
Even if you have done it before, it can still involve a lot of trial and error. 

This playbook shows you two paths to set up containerized vLLM to run a model distributed across the nodes ([see here for a single node](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/vllm)). 


## What you'll accomplish

Pick a path below to set up the cluster, distribute the model and make it available through an endpoint at `localhost` on your laptop.

- **Intermediate:** Use NVIDIA Sync to set up the cluster, then choose a model recipe and use NVIDIA provided scripts to set `spark-vllm-docker` to serve it (two Sparks).
- **Advanced:** Follow the manual instructions and use NVIDIA provided scripts (two Sparks).  

## What to know before starting

- Using [NVIDIA Sync](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/index.html) to connect to devices and launch an application. **Intermediate** 
- Choosing a model recipe and understanding model size, precision, and hardware fit. **Intermediate · Advanced**
- Reading Docker and Hugging Face CLI commands. **Intermediate · Advanced**
- Reading shell scripts and vLLM launch options, including tensor parallelism. **Advanced**

## Supported hardware platforms

The guided path supports two to four DGX Sparks. The command-line examples currently cover two.

| Hardware platform | OS | Memory per device | Beginner | Intermediate | Advanced |
| --- | --- | --- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Two DGX Sparks** | DGX OS (Linux) | 64 GB or 128 GB Unified Memory | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Three or four DGX Sparks** | DGX OS (Linux) | 64 GB or 128 GB Unified Memory | ✅ | — | — |

The dashes mean this draft has no worked command-line example for those cluster sizes.

Use DGX Sparks with the same memory size in one cluster: all 64 GB or all 128 GB.

## Prerequisites

**Hardware requirements**

- Two to four DGX Sparks with the necessary QSFP cables (switch required for four Sparks). **All paths**
- Two DGX Sparks for the current command-line examples. **Intermediate · Advanced**

**Software and access requirements**

- **Stop or rollback:** For Beginner, stop the model in NVIDIA Sync. For Intermediate and Advanced, stop the deployment on both Sparks from the head node before changing or deleting the cluster. Remove the cluster in NVIDIA Sync if you want to undo its network setup.

## Intermediate

## Run a vLLM model across two DGX Sparks

You will use NVIDIA Sync to set up a two-Spark cluster, then use a supplied recipe to run one model across both devices.

The recipe launcher starts a container on each Spark and runs vLLM across the pair.
You will send requests to the head Spark and use an SSH tunnel to reach its API from your laptop.

### Step 1. Connect and set up the two Sparks

**First, connect two Sparks with the same memory size.**

Use two 64GB Sparks or two 128GB Sparks.
Each recipe below is set for one of those pairs.

Follow the [Connect Multiple Sparks playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/connect-multiple-sparks) to cable the devices and set up the cluster with NVIDIA Sync.
Add both Sparks to Sync and allow it to set up the Docker group if prompted.

**Then, save the cluster's network details.**

Keep the head and worker addresses, SSH aliases, and ConnectX interface names from the cluster setup.
The launcher will use the ConnectX link to pass model data between the two Sparks.

**Success:** Both Sparks are in the cluster, and you can open a terminal on each through Sync.

### Step 2. Set up the launcher on the head Spark

**First, choose one Spark as the head and open its terminal through Sync.**

The head runs the API and starts the model on both devices.
Use this Spark for the rest of the commands unless a step says otherwise.

**Then, install `uv` and get the launcher.**

Run:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
git clone https://github.com/eugr/spark-vllm-docker.git
cd spark-vllm-docker
```

These are [community scripts](https://github.com/eugr/spark-vllm-docker) maintained outside NVIDIA.
The commands below use `uv` to run the recipe tool with its Python dependency.

**Next, find the cluster and check the saved settings.**

```bash
uv run --with pyyaml python run-recipe.py --discover
uv run --with pyyaml python run-recipe.py --show-env
```

Check that the saved `.env` file names exactly two Sparks, with this Spark first as the head.
Check the addresses and ConnectX interfaces against the details from Step 1.
If the launcher cannot reach the worker through SSH, fix that connection before you go on.

**Success:** The launcher has saved the intended head, worker, and network settings in `.env`.

### Step 3. Choose a model and save its recipe

**First, choose the row for your pair of Sparks.**

Memory in the table is **per Spark**.
These models use both devices to serve one endpoint.

| Cluster | Model | Recipe file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 × DGX Spark, 64GB each | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark-2gpu/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-flash-next&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=64&precision=fp4-local&memoryConfig=64) | [qwen38-flash-next-2x64gb.yaml](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm-cluster/assets/qwen38-flash-next-2x64gb.yaml) |
| 2 × DGX Spark, 128GB each | [GLM 5.3 Flash](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark-2gpu/index.html?model=z-ai%2Fglm-5.3-flash&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=128&precision=fp4-local&memoryConfig=128) | [glm53-flash-2x128gb.yaml](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm-cluster/assets/glm53-flash-2x128gb.yaml) |

**Then, save the recipe on the head Spark.**

1. Open the recipe file from your row
2. Copy its full contents into a file in the launcher's `recipes` folder on the head Spark
3. Use the file name shown in the table

For example, open this file in a text editor on the head Spark for the 64GB pair:

```bash
nano recipes/qwen38-flash-next-2x64gb.yaml
```

For the 128GB pair, use `recipes/glm53-flash-2x128gb.yaml` instead.
The supplied files keep the image, model, and serving settings from the matching NVIDIA recipe together.

**Success:** Your chosen recipe is saved in the head Spark's `recipes` folder.

### Step 4. Download the image and launch the model

**First, download the container image on the head Spark.**

Both recipes use this image:

```bash
docker pull eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:nightly-20261015
```

The recipe uses this tag so the model runs with the version of the backend it calls for.

**Then, run the command for your pair.**

For two 64GB Sparks:

```bash
uv run --with pyyaml python run-recipe.py recipes/qwen38-flash-next-2x64gb.yaml --setup
```

For two 128GB Sparks:

```bash
uv run --with pyyaml python run-recipe.py recipes/glm53-flash-2x128gb.yaml --setup
```

The setup step copies the prepared image and model files to the worker, then starts vLLM on both devices.
Allow time and free disk space on both Sparks for the image and model files.
If a model download asks for access, sign in on the head with `uvx hf auth login`, then run the command again.

**Next, keep the launch terminal open while the model runs.**

The first start can take a while as the model loads and the backend builds runtime files.
Wait for the head's logs to show that the API server has started.

**Success:** vLLM is running on both Sparks, and the head has started its API on port `8000`.

### Step 5. Check the API on the head Spark

**First, open a second terminal on the head through Sync.**

Leave the launch terminal open and run:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models
```

The health check should return HTTP `200`.
Copy the model ID from the model-list reply.
If the server is still loading, wait and try again.

**Then, send a chat request.**

Replace `<model-id>` with the ID from the model list:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about a GPU."}],"max_tokens":4096}'
```

These models may use some output tokens for reasoning before the final answer.
The larger output limit gives that work room to finish.

**Success:** The API returns a chat response with a final answer.

### Step 6. Reach the model from your laptop

**First, open a terminal on your laptop and start an SSH tunnel.**

Use the head Spark's management address or an SSH alias that works from your laptop.
Replace `<user>` and `<head-host>` below.
This command works in Windows PowerShell, macOS, and Linux terminals with OpenSSH installed:

```text
ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 <user>@<head-host>
```

Keep this terminal open.
The tunnel sends requests from port `8000` on your laptop to port `8000` on the head Spark.
Sync's cluster setup does not create this API tunnel.

If port `8000` is in use on your laptop, change the first `8000` to `8001` and use `8001` in your laptop's API URLs.

**Then, check the API from a second laptop terminal.**

| Laptop terminal | Health check | List served models |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows PowerShell | `curl.exe --fail-with-body -i http://localhost:8000/health` | `curl.exe --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models` |
| macOS or Linux | `curl --fail-with-body -i http://localhost:8000/health` | `curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models` |

For an OpenAI-compatible client on your laptop, use `http://localhost:8000/v1` as the base URL and the model ID from the list.
Both recipes support automatic tool calling; see the Advanced Tab for a test request.

**Success:** Your laptop can reach the model through the head Spark.

### Step 7. Stop and restart the model

**First, stop the model when you are done.**

Press `Ctrl+C` in the launch terminal on the head Spark.
The foreground launcher stops the containers on both Sparks when it exits.

You can also stop them from a second terminal on the head:

```bash
cd ~/spark-vllm-docker
./launch-cluster.sh stop
./launch-cluster.sh status
```

Close the laptop tunnel with `Ctrl+C` when you no longer need it.
The cluster's network settings and downloaded files stay in place.

**Then, restart with the same recipe when you need it again.**

From the repository on the head, run your Step 4 recipe command without `--setup`.
Keep that terminal open and start the laptop tunnel again if you need it.
Use `--setup` again if you need to restore missing model files or copy the image to the worker.
If the image is missing on the head, first run the `docker pull` command from Step 4 again.

**Success:** You can start and stop the model on both Sparks from the head.

## Advanced

## Run and tune a vLLM recipe across two DGX Sparks

You will run one vLLM service across two Sparks, using the Docker and server commands from an NVIDIA Local AI Inference Recipe.

This path uses SSH and a container on each node.
It covers the settings that split the model across the pair, move data between nodes, and set the capacity of the service.

### Step 1. Choose a model and prepare the cluster

**First, choose the recipe for your pair of Sparks.**

Memory in this table is per device.
Use two Sparks of the same memory size for these configurations.

| Cluster | Model and recipe | Checkpoint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 × DGX Spark, 64GB each | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark-2gpu/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-flash-next&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=64&precision=fp4-local&memoryConfig=64) | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` |
| 2 × DGX Spark, 128GB each | [GLM 5.3 Flash](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark-2gpu/index.html?model=z-ai%2Fglm-5.3-flash&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=128&precision=fp4-local&memoryConfig=128) | `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local` |

Both recipes use `eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:nightly-20261015`, a community image with the B12X backend.
Keep the image, checkpoint, environment settings, and server flags from the same recipe.
The 64GB Qwen configuration has its own memory settings; the settings for a pair of 128GB Sparks are different.

**Then, cable and configure the two nodes.**

Use **Configure Manually** in the [Connect Multiple Sparks playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/connect-multiple-sparks) if the cluster is not already set up.
Confirm interdevice SSH and Docker access on both nodes.
Choose a head Spark and a worker Spark, then open an SSH session to each.

Keep these values from the network setup:

| Value | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Head's ConnectX IP address | Rendezvous address shared by both vLLM processes |
| Each node's ConnectX Ethernet interface | Socket and control traffic on that node |
| Each node's RoCE HCA names | GPU data transfers over the cluster link |
| Head's management address or SSH alias | Laptop access to the API |

**Success:** You have a complete recipe and can reach both nodes over the cluster link.

### Step 2. Read the distributed and memory settings

**First, check how the recipe splits work across the pair.**

Each Spark runs one tensor-parallel rank.
The ranks hold parts of the model and exchange data during inference.
The head exposes the API; the worker joins the same service.
This gives you one model endpoint across two GPUs.

| Setting | Why it is in the command |
| --- | --- |
| `--tensor-parallel-size 2` | Splits supported model tensors across the two GPUs. Communication uses the link between the Sparks. |
| `--nnodes 2` | Sets the number of nodes in the distributed executor. |
| `--node-rank 0` or `1` | Gives each node a unique rank. The head is rank `0`. |
| `--master-addr` and `--master-port` | Set the shared rendezvous address and port. Use the head's ConnectX address on both nodes. |
| `--headless` | Runs the worker without an API server. |
| `--pipeline-parallel-size 1` | GLM keeps one pipeline stage; its model split uses tensor parallelism. |

These commands use native multi-node execution.
They do not need a separate Ray cluster.
API port `8000` and rendezvous port `29501` serve different roles.
See the [vLLM multi-node multiprocessing guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/parallelism_scaling/#running-vllm-with-multiprocessing) for the rank and rendezvous settings.

**Next, check the memory and scheduling limits.**

Each node must fit its share of the weights, caches, and runtime work.
The pair does not act as one flat pool of memory.

| Setting | Why it is in the recipe |
| --- | --- |
| `--quantization modelopt_mixed` and `--load-format b12x` | Select the weight format and loader supported by the checkpoint and image. |
| `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` | Sets KV-cache precision apart from weight precision. |
| `--gpu-memory-utilization` | Sets the fraction of GPU memory vLLM budgets for its executor on each node. |
| `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 3G` | Gives Qwen an explicit KV-cache budget per GPU. This takes precedence over the utilization setting for KV-cache sizing. |
| `--max-model-len` | Caps the total input and output tokens in one request. |
| `--max-num-seqs` | Caps the number of sequences processed in one iteration. |
| `--max-num-batched-tokens` | Sets the token budget for one scheduler iteration. |
| `--enable-chunked-prefill` | Lets long prompt processing share batches with decode work. |
| `--enable-prefix-caching` | Reuses cached prompt work when requests share a prefix. |

The context limit is a per-request ceiling.
It does not mean every active request can use that full length at once.
Actual capacity also depends on the model's cache layout and the other requests in flight.

**Then, keep the model-specific backend settings together for the first run.**

The B12X kernels, compilation settings, and environment variables are part of these recipes.
For example, the 64GB Qwen recipe uses `VLLM_PLE_TABLE_MEMORY=disk`, limits compile workers, and sets a `3G` KV-cache budget.
GLM uses a different attention backend, block size, and memory budget.

Both recipes use native multi-token prediction (MTP) for speculative decoding.
They do not call for a separate draft checkpoint.
Keep the reasoning and tool-call parsers if the service will be used by an agent.

See the [vLLM serve options](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/cli/serve/), [memory and scheduling guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/), and [speculative decoding guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/) for the core settings.
The community image supplies the B12X-specific code paths used here.

**Success:** You know which settings define the cluster, which set its capacity, and which belong to the chosen model and backend.

### Step 3. Start a container on each Spark

**First, set the network values in each node's host shell.**

Use the same head address and rendezvous port on both nodes.
Set `ETH_IF` and `IB_IF` to the local node's interfaces; their names may differ between nodes.
Keep both RoCE HCA names called for by the recipe.

```bash
export HEAD_IP="<head-connectx-ip>"
export ETH_IF="<local-connectx-interface>"
export IB_IF="<local-roce-hca-1>,<local-roce-hca-2>"
export MASTER_PORT=29501
export IMAGE="eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:nightly-20261015"
export HF_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/huggingface"
```

**Then, run this Docker command on each node.**

If checkpoint access needs a Hugging Face token, set `HF_TOKEN` in the host shell first.
The container downloads the image if needed, and vLLM downloads the model when it starts.
Both nodes need the model files and enough free disk space for their local caches.

```bash
mkdir -p "$HF_CACHE_DIR" "$HOME/.cache/vllm" \
  "$HOME/.cache/flashinfer" "$HOME/.triton" "$HOME/.cache/b12x"

docker run --rm -it \
  --name vllm_cluster \
  --privileged --gpus all --ipc host --network host \
  --shm-size=16g \
  --ulimit nofile=1048576:1048576 \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -e HF_TOKEN="${HF_TOKEN:-}" \
  -e MN_IF_NAME="$ETH_IF" -e UCX_NET_DEVICES="$ETH_IF" \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME="$ETH_IF" -e NCCL_IB_HCA="$IB_IF" \
  -e NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 -e NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1 \
  -e OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include="$ETH_IF" \
  -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME="$ETH_IF" -e TP_SOCKET_IFNAME="$ETH_IF" \
  -e HEAD_IP="$HEAD_IP" -e MASTER_PORT="$MASTER_PORT" \
  -v "$HF_CACHE_DIR:/root/.cache/huggingface" \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/vllm:/root/.cache/vllm" \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/flashinfer:/root/.cache/flashinfer" \
  -v "$HOME/.triton:/root/.triton" \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/b12x:/root/.cache/b12x" \
  --entrypoint /bin/bash "$IMAGE"
```

Host networking and the interface variables let the processes use the ConnectX link.
The mounts keep model and runtime files across container restarts.
The API will bind to the head's host interfaces, so use the service on your trusted network.

**Success:** You have an open Bash shell inside the container on each node.

### Step 4. Run the model on the head and worker

**First, set the rank arguments inside each container.**

On the head, run:

```bash
NODE_ARGS=(--node-rank 0)
```

On the worker, run:

```bash
NODE_ARGS=(--node-rank 1 --headless)
```

**Then, run the full command for your model in both containers.**

Use the same model, environment settings, and serving flags on both nodes.
Only the rank arguments differ.
Start the head command, then start the worker command in its session; the distributed startup waits for both ranks.

#### Qwen3.8 Flash-Next on two 64GB Sparks

export CUTE_DSL_ARCH="sm_121a"
export SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU="1"
export VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD="spawn"

vllm serve nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \

  --trust-remote-code \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --mamba-cache-mode align \
  --enable-prefix-caching \

### Step 5. Test the API and tool calling

**First, check readiness from a second host shell on the head.**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models
```

Wait for HTTP `200`, then copy the model ID from the model list.
If startup fails, check both container sessions: a worker failure can block the head.

**Next, send a chat request with that model ID.**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about a GPU."}],"max_tokens":4096}'
```

Allow enough output tokens for reasoning and a final answer.
Check `finish_reason` if the response stops before the answer is complete.

**Then, test automatic tool calling.**

Replace `<model-id>` and run:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Use get_weather to look up the weather in Boston."}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","description":"Get current weather for a location.","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"location":{"type":"string"}},"required":["location"]}}}],"tool_choice":"auto","max_tokens":4096}'
```

Look for a `tool_calls` entry for `get_weather` with Boston in its arguments, and `finish_reason` set to `tool_calls`.
The request declares the tool; your client would execute it.
If the reply is plain text, check the model's tool support, chat template, and parser settings.
See the [vLLM tool-calling guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/tool_calling/).

**Success:** Chat and automatic tool calling work through the head's API.

### Step 6. Connect a client and tune the workload

**First, forward the head's API port to your laptop if needed.**

Run this in a local laptop terminal, using the head's management address or a working SSH alias:

```text
ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 <user>@<head-host>
```

Keep the tunnel open and use `http://localhost:8000/v1` as the client's base URL.
Set the client's model to the ID from `/v1/models`.
The worker does not need a separate client connection.

**Then, measure the service with prompts and concurrency that match your workload.**

Record prompt length, output length, active requests, time to first token, and output tokens per second.
Watch memory and link use on both Sparks.
Two nodes add capacity and communication work; measure the result for the model and request mix you plan to serve.

Change one setting at a time and apply the same change on both ranks.

| Goal | Settings to review |
| --- | --- |
| Fit the workload within memory | Active sequences, context length, and the recipe's KV-cache budget |
| Change the balance between prompt work and active replies | `--max-num-batched-tokens` with chunked prefill |
| Reuse repeated prompt text | Prefix caching with matching system prompts or document prefixes |
| Check the benefit of MTP | Compare the recipe's speculative settings with a supported baseline under the same request mix |

Keep a copy of the working commands, image tag or digest, checkpoint revision, network values, and measurements before you tune.

**Success:** You have a working client and a measured baseline for further changes.

### Step 7. Stop or save the service

**First, stop both containers when you are done.**

Run this from a host shell on **each Spark**:

```bash
docker stop vllm_cluster
```

The containers are removed when they stop.
The mounted model and runtime caches remain for the next start.
Close the laptop tunnel with `Ctrl+C`.

**Then, save the host and server commands if you want a repeatable launch.**

Keep the per-node network values and rank arguments with the full model command.
If you use a wrapper, have it start and stop both ranks and report a failed worker.
The Intermediate Tab includes supplied YAML recipes for the community launcher; those files keep the model environment and serve flags together while the launcher supplies the node ranks and starts both containers.

**Success:** Both nodes have stopped, and you have the commands needed to start the same service again.

## Troubleshooting

## Common issues

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cluster Assistant cannot finish its checks | One or both Sparks or their ConnectX-7 link needs attention | Return to [Connect Multiple DGX Sparks](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/connect-multiple-sparks) and complete its checks before running the recipe. |
| `docker` reports permission denied on either Spark | The device user cannot access Docker | Follow the Docker access check in the [single-device instructions](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/vllm/intermediate). |
| Model download reports an authentication error | Hugging Face CLI access is missing or invalid on a Spark | Check `hf auth whoami` on both devices and authenticate as described in the [Hugging Face guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/main/en/quick-start#authentication). |
| The API does not respond on the head Spark | The recipe may still be loading or launch may have failed | Check the output in the launch terminal before retrying the `/health` request. |

The cluster recipe and manual launcher have separate setup steps. Use the commands from one path consistently; see **Intermediate** for the recipe or **Advanced** for explicit launch settings.

## Overview

## Basic idea

[vLLM](https://vllm.ai/) is a high-performance inference engine for serving LLMs at datacenter scale.
However, getting the desired performance requires significant background knowledge and configuration experience, especially when setting up on a local system.

This playbook shows you two paths to set up vLLM and configure the endpoint on a remote DGX Spark or DGX Station ([for a Spark cluster, go here](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/vllm-cluster)). 


## What you'll accomplish

- **Intermediate:** Manually prepare a recommended model on the remote device and configure the vLLM container as an NVIDIA Sync Custom App.
- **Advanced:** Get under the hood and do everything manually to learn about vLLM and optimize model performance.

## What to know before starting

- How to use [NVIDIA Sync](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/index.html). **Intermediate**
- How to read Docker and Hugging Face CLI commands. **Intermediate · Advanced**
- How to read and edit a Bash launch script. **Intermediate · Advanced**
- How to choose a model recipe and understanding model size and precision. **Advanced**
- How to configure `docker run` and `vllm serve` arguments. **Advanced**

## Supported hardware platforms

Check the table below to confirm which path this playbook supports for your hardware.

| Hardware platform | OS | Memory | One device |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :----: |
| **DGX Spark** | DGX OS (Linux) | 64 GB or 128 GB Unified Memory | ✅ |
| **DGX Station** | Ubuntu (Linux) | Large HBM + Grace DRAM | ✅ |

## Prerequisites

**Hardware requirements**

- One DGX Spark or DGX Station. 

**Software and access requirements**

- [NVIDIA Sync installed](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/getting-started.html#installation-and-onboarding) on your laptop, with the DGX device [connected](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/direct-connections.html#adding-a-device-for-a-direct-connection). **Intermediate** 
- Docker installed on the DGX device and [available to your user](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/#add-your-user-to-the-docker-group). **Intermediate · Advanced**
- An [installed](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/main/en/guides/cli#standalone-installer-recommended) Hugging Face CLI on the remote device. **Intermediate · Advanced**
- SSH access to the remote device. **Advanced**

## Time & risk

- **Estimated time:** Intermediate varies between 15 and 30 minutes depending on network speed. Advanced takes about 30 minutes more to account for manual steps.
- **Risk level:** Low
- **Stop or rollback:** You can stop configuration flows at any time, and you can remove the container or model from the device manually.
- **Last Updated:** 10/19/2026
  - Intermediate offers two models per device and memory size, with matching NVIDIA Sync launch scripts
  - Advanced combines Spark and Station in one recipe workflow, with explanations of memory, scheduling, and model settings
  - Advanced includes API and tool-call checks, manual launch scripts, and client setup for Hermes, OpenShell, and laptop access

## Intermediate

## Set up a vLLM container as an NVIDIA Sync custom app

You will use NVIDIA Sync to connect to a DGX Spark or Station, then download a vLLM container and a model for your device.

Then, you will add a supplied launch script as a custom app in NVIDIA Sync.
Once the app is set up, you can use Sync to start and stop the model and reach its API from your laptop.

Sync sets up the SSH tunnel and port forwarding for you.

### Step 1. Install NVIDIA Sync on your laptop

**First, download NVIDIA Sync for your laptop.**

NVIDIA Sync is a desktop app that lets you connect to a remote Linux device and run apps on it.

::spark-download

**Then, install and open NVIDIA Sync.**

**For Windows:** Double-click the `.exe` installer and follow the steps.

**For macOS:** Open `nvidia-sync.dmg`, drag the app into Applications, then open it.

**For Ubuntu:** Follow the [Ubuntu install steps](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/getting-started.html#installation).

**Success:** NVIDIA Sync opens on your laptop.

### Step 2. Add your DGX Spark or Station to NVIDIA Sync

**First, choose how to add your device.**

Your laptop must be able to reach the device on the network.
You can add it in one of three ways:

1. **mDNS:** Select a device that Sync finds on the network, then enter your username and password
2. **Manual:** Select **Add a device manually**, enter the device's IP address, then enter your username and password
3. **Import:** Select a working SSH alias from your local SSH config, then add it

For mDNS or Manual, have these details ready:

- **Name:** a name to help you find the device in Sync
- **Hostname or IP:** the device's network name or IP address
- **Username:** your username on the device
- **Password:** the password for that user

> [!NOTE]
> If you use an SSH key to sign in, first set up an SSH alias, then import it into Sync. See [Add a device for a direct connection](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/direct-connections.html#adding-a-device-for-a-direct-connection).

**Then, allow NVIDIA Sync to set up the Docker group if prompted.**

If Sync asks to add your user to the `docker` group, click **Confirm**.
This lets the launch script run Docker as your user.
You will need `sudo` access for this step.

> [!NOTE]
> Access to the `docker` group grants root access without a password, which is a risk. Learn more in the [Docker user guide](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/#manage-docker-as-a-non-root-user).

**Success:** Your device appears in NVIDIA Sync.

### Step 3. Connect, open a terminal and check the tools

**First, connect to the device and open a terminal.**

1. Select your device from the NVIDIA Sync drop-down
2. Click **Connect**
3. Select the **Terminal** app

The terminal opens an SSH session on the DGX device.
You will run the download commands in this terminal.

**Then, check that the Hugging Face CLI is installed.**

Run:

```bash
hf --help
```

If it returns `command not found`, install the CLI with the [Hugging Face install steps](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/main/en/guides/cli#standalone-installer-recommended), then open a new terminal.

**Success:** `hf --help` shows the CLI help.

### Step 4. Choose a model and download its files

**First, choose one of the two rows for your device and memory size.**

Each row has a matching launch script in Step 5.
The recipe links give you more detail about the model settings used by these scripts.

| Device | Memory | Model | Docker pull command | Model download command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DGX Spark | 64GB unified memory | [Qwen3.8 27B (NVFP4)](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-27b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=64&precision=nvfp4&variant=&memoryConfig=64) | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:v0.28.0` | `hf download nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` |
| DGX Spark | 64GB unified memory | [Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B A9B](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=nvidia%2Fnemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=64&precision=iq2&variant=&memoryConfig=64) | `docker pull eugr/spark-vllm:nightly-20261016` | `hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB` |
| DGX Spark | 128GB unified memory | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-flash-next&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=128&precision=fp4-local&variant=&memoryConfig=128) | `docker pull eugr/spark-vllm-b12x:nightly-20261015` | `hf download nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` |
| DGX Spark | 128GB unified memory | [Qwen3.8 27B (NVFP4)](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-27b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=128&precision=nvfp4&variant=&memoryConfig=128) | `docker pull nvcr.io/nvidia/vllm:26.10.pre1-py3` | `hf download nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` |
| DGX Station | 748GB coherent memory | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-station/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-flash-next&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=&precision=nvfp4&variant=&memoryConfig=748) | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next` | `hf download Inferact/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` |
| DGX Station | 748GB coherent memory | [Nemotron 3 Super 120B A12B](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-station/index.html?model=nvidia%2Fnemotron-3-super-120b-a12b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=&precision=nvfp4&variant=mtp&memoryConfig=748) | `docker pull vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0` | `hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-NVFP4` |


**Next, download the container and model on the DGX device.**

1. Run the `docker pull` command from your row and wait for it to finish
2. Run the `hf download` command from the same row and wait for it to finish

> [!NOTE]
> You can speed up the model download by temporarily setting `HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1` in the download command, i.e. `HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1 hf download <model>`. 

**If you selected Qwen3.8 27B or Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, download the draft model needed for speculative decoding.**

The Qwen3.8 27B and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt scripts use a second, smaller model to help speed up replies through something called "[speculative decoding](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/an-introduction-to-speculative-decoding-for-reducing-latency-in-ai-inference/)".

Run the command for your model below.

| Model | Draft model download command |
| --- | --- |
| Qwen3.8 27B, on either Spark memory size | `hf download z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` |
| Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B A9B | `hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-LiLiCorr` |

> [!NOTE]
> The container and model files are large. Check that the device has enough free disk space and allow time for all downloads to finish.

**Success:** The container, model and any draft model have finished downloading.

### Step 5. Add the model to NVIDIA Sync

**First, open the launch script for the row you chose in Step 4.**

Each script starts the container and runs the model with the recipe's settings. It also stops the container when you stop the app in Sync.

| Device | Memory | App name | Launch script |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DGX Spark | 64GB | `vLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-64GB` | [Qwen3.8 27B on 64GB Spark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-spark-64gb-qwen38-27b.sh) |
| DGX Spark | 64GB | `vLLM-Nemotron3.5-Bolt` | [Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on 64GB Spark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-spark-64gb-nemotron35-bolt.sh) |
| DGX Spark | 128GB | `vLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next on 128GB Spark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-spark-128gb-qwen38-flash-next.sh) |
| DGX Spark | 128GB | `vLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-128GB` | [Qwen3.8 27B on 128GB Spark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-spark-128gb-qwen38-27b.sh) |
| DGX Station | 748GB | `vLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` | [Qwen3.8 Flash-Next on Station](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-station-qwen38-flash-next.sh) |
| DGX Station | 748GB | `vLLM-Nemotron3-Super` | [Nemotron 3 Super on Station](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks/refs/heads/main/nvidia/playbook-vllm/assets/sync-vllm-station-nemotron3-super.sh) |

**Then, add the script as a custom app.**

1. In NVIDIA Sync, connect to your device
2. Select **Custom** > **+ Add New**
3. Enter the **App name** from your row in **Name**, and enter `8000` in **Port**
4. Paste the full script into **Launch Script**
5. Leave **Auto open** and **Launch in Terminal** off, and leave **URL Path** blank
6. Select **Add**

Learn more about [Sync custom apps](https://docs.nvidia.com/sync/latest/applications.html#custom-scripts-and-applications).

> [!NOTE]
> Start with one model app at a time. If port `8000` is in use, choose a free port, such as `8001`. Set both the Sync app's **Port** and `PORT=8000` near the top of its launch script to that number. Use the same port in the laptop commands in Step 7.

**Success:** The app appears in the **Custom** section for your device.

### Step 6. Launch the app and watch the server start

**First, click the app name in NVIDIA Sync.**

The script starts the container and loads the model. Sync forwards the model's API port to your laptop.

**Next, open the resource monitor to watch the device.**

1. Click the resource monitor in NVIDIA Sync
2. Select the views to see CPU, GPU and memory use as the server starts

The first start can take a while as vLLM builds runtime files and loads the model. Device activity shows that work is in progress; use Step 7 to check that the API is ready.

**Then, check the container logs in a terminal on the DGX device.**

Open **Terminal** through Sync and run the command for your app.

| App name | Log command |
| --- | --- |
| `vLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-64GB` | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-spark-64gb-qwen38-27b` |
| `vLLM-Nemotron3.5-Bolt` | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-spark-64gb-nemotron35-bolt` |
| `vLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` (128GB DGX Spark) | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-spark-128gb-qwen38-flash-next` |
| `vLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-128GB` | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-spark-128gb-qwen38-27b` |
| `vLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` (DGX Station) | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-station-qwen38-flash-next` |
| `vLLM-Nemotron3-Super` | `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-station-nemotron3-super` |

Press `Ctrl+C` to leave the log view. The model app keeps running.

**Success:** The logs show the server is ready to accept requests. Continue to Step 7 to check the API and send a request.

### Step 7. Test the API from your laptop

**First, open a local terminal on your laptop and check the server.**

Keep the model app running and Sync connected.
Use the commands for your laptop below.
If you chose a port other than `8000`, use that port in each URL.

1. Run the health check and look for HTTP `200`
2. Run the model-list command and copy the model ID from the reply

| Laptop terminal | Health check | List served models |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Windows PowerShell | `curl.exe --fail-with-body -i http://localhost:8000/health` | `curl.exe --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models` |
| macOS or Linux | `curl --fail-with-body -i http://localhost:8000/health` | `curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models` |

If the health check cannot connect while the model loads, wait and try again. Check the container logs if startup fails.

**Then, use the model ID to send a chat request.**

1. Copy the chat command for your laptop
2. Replace `<model-id>` with the exact ID returned by `/v1/models`
3. Run the command and wait for the reply

| Laptop terminal | Chat request |
| --- | --- |
| Windows PowerShell | `(Invoke-RestMethod -Uri http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -Method Post -ContentType "application/json" -Body '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about a GPU."}],"max_tokens":4096}').choices` |
| macOS or Linux | `curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a haiku about a GPU."}],"max_tokens":4096}'` |

**Success:** The response has a `choices` array with the model's answer. Your laptop can now reach the model through Sync.

### Step 8. Stop the model and start it again

**First, stop the app through NVIDIA Sync.**

1. Open the NVIDIA Sync pop-up window
2. Click the **x** beside the running custom app

The supplied script stops and removes its container. The model files and cached runtime files stay on the DGX device for the next start.

**Then, start the model when you need it again.**

1. Connect to the device through Sync
2. Click the custom app name
3. Wait for the model to load, then run the health check from Step 7

**Success:** The health check returns HTTP `200` again. You can start and stop this model through Sync each time you need it.

### Next steps

- Connect an app on your laptop to `http://localhost:8000/v1`, using the model ID from Step 7. Use your chosen port if you changed it.
- Continue to the Advanced tab to learn how to choose and run a recipe yourself.
- Use the Troubleshooting Tab if the app fails to start or your laptop cannot reach the API.
- Use [the vLLM cluster playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/vllm-cluster) to serve across more than one DGX Spark.

## Advanced

## Choose and run a vLLM recipe on DGX Spark or Station

You will choose a recipe for your device, run its commands, and test the model's API and tool calling.

Along the way, you will see how the recipe uses memory, batches requests, and selects the code that runs the model.

Once the endpoint works, you can tune it for your workload, save the launch command, and use it with a client such as Hermes or OpenShell.

### Step 1. Choose a model and recipe

**First, open the recipe page for your device and memory size.**

Use [NVIDIA Local AI Inference Recipes](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/) to select a model and vLLM configuration.

| Device | Memory | Recommended model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DGX Spark | 64GB unified memory | [Qwen3.8 27B (NVFP4)](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-27b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=64&precision=nvfp4&variant=&memoryConfig=64) |
| DGX Spark | 128GB unified memory | [Qwen3.8 27B (NVFP4)](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-spark/index.html?model=qwen%2Fqwen3.8-27b&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=128&precision=nvfp4&variant=&memoryConfig=128) |
| DGX Station | 748GB coherent memory | [DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-station/index.html?model=deepseek%2Fdeepseek-v4-flash-0731&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=&precision=fp4-fp8-mixed&variant=&memoryConfig=748) | 

The recommended Spark model is also one of the models in the Intermediate tab, so you can use either path.
If you pick a different model in the recipe page, check its prerequisites before you download it.

**Then, copy the "Start container" and "Launch" commands and save them to a file.**


The checkpoint, image, environment settings, and server flags work together.
For example, a low-precision checkpoint needs a backend that can load and run its format, and a speculative-decoding variant may need a second checkpoint.
Start with the full configuration from one recipe.

> [!NOTE]
> [DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 on Station](https://nvidia.github.io/local-ai-inference-recipes/hardware/dgx-station/index.html?model=deepseek%2Fdeepseek-v4-flash-0731&os=linux&backend=vllm&memory=&precision=fp4-fp8-mixed&variant=&memoryConfig=748) is the recommended Station recipe. The recipe page marks it experimental. Its setup command uses `--gpus all`, so on a Station with more than one GPU, select the GB300 as described in Step 3. Keep the recipe's setup and launch commands together.

**Success:** You have saved a complete recipe for your device and chosen model.

### Step 2. Read the settings that shape the service

**First, check how the recipe divides memory between weights and requests.**

The model weights take up part of the device's memory.
Serving also needs space for runtime work and the KV cache, which holds attention keys and values from tokens already processed.
Longer requests and more requests in flight compete for that space.

| Setting | Why it is in the recipe |
| --- | --- |
| Checkpoint precision and `--quantization` | Set how model weights are stored and run. Lower precision can reduce weight memory use; the checkpoint and backend must support it. |
| `--gpu-memory-utilization` | Sets the fraction of GPU memory vLLM budgets for its executor. A higher value can leave more room for KV cache, with less headroom for other use. |
| `--max-model-len` | Caps the total input and output tokens in a request. A large limit needs enough cache to serve long requests. |
| `--max-num-seqs` | Caps the number of sequences processed in one iteration. More active sequences can raise throughput and memory use. |
| `--kv-cache-dtype` | Sets KV-cache precision separately from weight precision. A supported lower-precision cache can hold more tokens in the same memory. |
| `--cpu-offload-gb` | Places some model weights in host memory. This can make a large model fit, with performance tied to host memory and the CPU–GPU link. |

See the [vLLM serve options](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/cli/serve/) and [quantized KV-cache guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/quantization/quantized_kvcache/) for details.

**Next, check how the recipe schedules work and reuses it.**

vLLM first processes the input prompt, called *prefill*, then generates output tokens, called *decode*.
The best settings depend on prompt length, output length, and the number of clients.

| Setting | Why it is in the recipe |
| --- | --- |
| `--max-num-batched-tokens` | Sets the token budget for one scheduler iteration. With chunked prefill, smaller values can help active replies keep moving; larger values can process more prompt tokens at once. |
| `--enable-chunked-prefill` | Splits long prompt processing into chunks that can share batches with decode work. |
| `--enable-prefix-caching` | Reuses cached work for shared prompt prefixes, such as repeated system prompts or document text. It saves prompt work when the prefix matches. |
| `--speculative-config` | Uses a draft model or native prediction heads to propose tokens for the main model to check. The gain depends on the model and workload. Preserve any draft-checkpoint settings. |

Read more about [scheduling and tuning](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/), [prefix caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/automatic_prefix_caching/), and [speculative decoding](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/).

**Then, keep the recipe's model-specific runtime settings together.**

Load formats, attention and MoE backends, compilation settings, and environment variables select code paths supported by that image and model.
Keep them for the first run so you have a working baseline.

For agent use, also keep the model's tool-call and reasoning parsers.
`--enable-auto-tool-choice` allows the model to choose a tool, while `--tool-call-parser` reads its tool-call format.
`--reasoning-parser` separates reasoning from the final answer; the model's chat template and request settings control whether it thinks.
See [tool calling](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/tool_calling/) and [reasoning outputs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/reasoning_outputs/).

**Success:** You know which settings control capacity, scheduling, and the response format your client will receive.

### Step 3. Run the recipe

**First, check the setup command in a terminal on the DGX device.**

Use a local terminal on the device or an SSH session.
Set any host variables called for by the recipe, such as `HF_TOKEN`.

**For Station, check that the command selects the GB300.**

If the recipe uses `--gpus all` and your Station has more than one GPU, get the GB300's ID on the host:

```bash
GB300_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --format=csv,noheader | \
  awk -F, 'tolower($2) ~ /gb300/ {gsub(/[[:space:]]/, "", $1); print $1; exit}')
: "${GB300_UUID:?No GB300 found}"
```

Before running the container, replace `--gpus all` with `--gpus "device=${GB300_UUID}"`.
Keep any GPU selection already supplied by the recipe.

**Then, run the full setup command on the DGX host.**

Docker pulls the image if it is missing.
The setup or server command downloads model files as needed; keep any explicit download, revision, and local-path options in the recipe.

The image supplies the vLLM build and libraries used by the configuration.
The Hugging Face cache mount keeps model files on the host.
Mounts for the vLLM, FlashInfer, and Triton caches also let later containers reuse compiled work.
First startup can include downloads, compilation, and kernel tuning.

**Next, run the server command inside the container.**

A setup command that ends with `--entrypoint /bin/bash` and an image name opens a shell in that image.
In that shell:

1. Apply any listed environment settings
2. Run the complete `vllm serve` command
3. Leave the terminal open and follow startup output

If the recipe already launches the server in its Docker command, follow that form directly.

**Finally, note the API address and port.**

With `--network host`, vLLM listens directly on the DGX host's port.
With a Docker `-p` mapping, use the published host port for checks outside the container.
With host networking, a loopback bind is enough for host-local clients and SSH forwarding.
With port mapping, keep vLLM bound to `0.0.0.0` inside the container and choose the host-side bind in the mapping.
The OpenShell handoff in Step 7 needs the service reachable from its sandbox.

The commands below use DGX host port `8000`.
Use your recipe's host port if it differs.

**Success:** The server reports that it is ready to accept requests. Confirm readiness with the API checks in Step 4.

### Step 4. Test inference and tool calling

**First, open a second terminal on the DGX device and check the API.**

Run:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -i http://localhost:8000/health
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/models
```

The health check should return HTTP `200`, and the model list should have a non-empty `data` array.
Copy the served model's `id` for the requests below.
It can differ from the checkpoint name when the recipe sets `--served-model-name`.

**Then, send a chat request with that model ID.**

Replace `<model-id>` and run:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with a short greeting."}],"max_tokens":4096}'
```

**Success:** `choices[0].message.content` contains an answer.
Reasoning can use the output-token budget before an answer appears; follow the recipe's request settings or raise the budget if the response ends with `finish_reason: length`.

> [!NOTE]
> For DeepSeek V4 Flash, add `"chat_template_kwargs":{"thinking":false}` to the JSON body of both tests here for a check with reasoning off. Reasoning controls differ by model; use the selected model's settings.

**Finally, test a tool call.**

Replace `<model-id>` and run:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"<model-id>","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Use get_weather to look up the weather in Boston."}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather","description":"Get current weather for a location.","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"location":{"type":"string"}},"required":["location"]}}}],"tool_choice":"auto","max_tokens":4096}'
```

**Success:** The response contains a `tool_calls` entry for `get_weather` with Boston in its arguments, and `finish_reason` is `tool_calls`.
This checks the model's automatic tool-call path and response format; the request declares the tool, and your client would execute it.
If the model replies in plain text, check the recipe's tool-call settings and the chosen model's tool support.

### Step 5. (optional) Tune the service for your workload

**First, record a baseline with representative requests.**

Use the prompt lengths, output lengths, and client count you expect to serve.
Record time to first token, output tokens per second, and memory use.
For multiple clients, distinguish each client's generation rate from total throughput.

**Then, change one setting and repeat the same workload.**

1. Set `--max-model-len` to cover your actual input and output needs
2. Try `--max-num-seqs` and `--max-num-batched-tokens` to balance concurrency and latency
3. Compare repeated-prefix workloads with prefix caching, or test the recipe's speculative-decoding variant
4. Keep the settings that improve your target measure, then rerun the chat and tool tests

Memory capacity, request length, and concurrency form a shared budget.
A context limit of 262144 tokens and `--max-num-seqs 8` do not guarantee that eight full-length requests fit at once.
Read the KV-cache capacity and concurrency estimates in startup output, then test the load you intend to run.

**Success:** You have measured settings that suit your workload and still pass the functional checks.

### Step 6. (optional) Save a repeatable launch script

**First, save the working host setup and server commands.**

Keep the image tag, checkpoint revision or path, GPU selection, cache mounts, environment settings, and tested vLLM options together.

**Then, combine the commands if you want one launch script.**

For a recipe that opens `/bin/bash` before you run `vllm serve`:

1. Move the server's environment settings into Docker `-e NAME=value` options
2. Replace `--entrypoint /bin/bash` with `--entrypoint vllm`
3. After the image name, append `serve`, the checkpoint or path, and the tested server arguments
4. Keep any host preparation before `docker run`, including recipe-specific downloads or cache setup
5. Add a container name, such as `--name vllm-local`, and save the result as `launch-vllm.sh`

Make it executable and run it on the DGX device:

```bash
chmod +x launch-vllm.sh
./launch-vllm.sh
```

For a background service, replace the interactive `-it` options with `-d`.
Follow its output with `docker logs --tail 50 --follow vllm-local` and stop it with `docker stop vllm-local`.
If the recipe uses `--rm`, run the saved script again to create the next container.

**Success:** The saved script starts the same service and passes the checks in Step 4.

### Step 7. Connect Hermes, OpenShell, or a laptop client

**First, use an API address reachable from your client.**

Keep the server running and use the exact model ID returned by `/v1/models`.

| Client | API base URL | Setup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hermes or another process on the DGX host | `http://localhost:8000/v1` | Follow the client setup with the served model ID. |
| A client on your laptop | `http://localhost:8000/v1` | Forward a local port to the DGX host port with SSH, as shown below. |
| The OpenShell sandbox in its playbook | `http://host.openshell.internal:8000/v1` | Keep vLLM reachable from the sandbox; the playbook uses `--host 0.0.0.0` and host port `8000`. |

The recipe's `0.0.0.0` bind can expose an unauthenticated API on the device's network interfaces.
Use a trusted network or suitable access controls for that route.

**For a laptop client, open an SSH tunnel from the laptop.**

Replace `user@dgx-host` with your SSH login and device address, then run:

```bash
ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 user@dgx-host
```

Keep the tunnel open, then run the health and model-list checks from a second laptop terminal.
Use `curl.exe` for those checks in Windows PowerShell.
If laptop port `8000` is busy, change the leftmost port to `8001` and use `http://localhost:8001/v1` in the client.

**For Hermes or OpenShell, continue with the matching playbook.**

- In the [Hermes playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/hermes-agent), use the host-local API URL and the served model ID. For DeepSeek, follow that playbook's model-specific reasoning settings.
- In the [OpenShell playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/openshell), reuse this endpoint and continue at Step 6 after exporting `MODEL_HANDLE` as in its Step 5. Use the ID from `/v1/models`; the recipe may give the service an alias.

**Success:** Your client reaches the existing vLLM service and uses the model you tested.

### Next steps

- Use the Troubleshooting Tab for startup, memory, or connection errors.
- Review the [vLLM tuning guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/) for further performance work.
- Use [the vLLM cluster playbook](https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/vllm-cluster) for more than one DGX Spark.

## Troubleshooting

## Common issues

The **Applies to** column identifies the relevant path and hardware. "All paths · all hardware platforms" applies throughout this playbook.

| Symptom | Applies to | Cause | Fix |
|---------|------------|-------|-----|
| "permission denied" when running docker | Advanced · all hardware platforms | User not in docker group | Run `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER && newgrp docker` |
| Container fails to start with GPU error | All paths · all hardware platforms | NVIDIA Container Toolkit not configured | Run `nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` and restart Docker |
| CUDA out of memory | All paths · all hardware platforms | Other models are still running, or the model settings need more memory than is free | For Intermediate, stop other model apps in Sync and check that the launch script matches your device and memory size in Steps 4 and 5. For Advanced, reduce context length or concurrency in the selected recipe, or choose a smaller model or lower-precision checkpoint. |
| Model or draft-model files are missing | Intermediate · all hardware platforms | A download did not finish, the wrong launch script was chosen, or the files were downloaded under another user or cache path | Finish the downloads in Step 4, including the draft model for Qwen3.8 27B or Nemotron 3.5 Bolt. Use the matching script from Step 5 and the same DGX user for downloads and Sync. If you use `HF_HOME`, check that the script uses the same path as the downloads. |
| `Could not find a GB300 GPU with nvidia-smi.` | Intermediate · DGX Station | The script cannot find the Station's GB300 | Check that Sync is connected to the right Station. Run `nvidia-smi` on that device and confirm it lists a GB300 before trying again. |
| Port 8000 is in use | Intermediate · Advanced | Another app is using the port on the laptop or DGX device | Stop the other app, or follow the instructions for your path under **Use another API port** below. |
| Laptop cannot reach the API, but `/health` returns HTTP `200` on the DGX device | Intermediate · Advanced | Port forwarding is not active or uses a different port | For Intermediate, keep Sync connected and the custom app running. Check that the Sync app's **Port**, the script's `PORT`, and the laptop URL use the same port. Run the laptop checks in a local terminal as shown in Step 7. For Advanced, check the forwarding route for your client. On Windows, run PowerShell commands in PowerShell rather than WSL unless you have configured forwarding there. |
| PowerShell prompts for `Uri` when you enter a `curl` command | Intermediate · Advanced | `curl` is a PowerShell alias for `Invoke-WebRequest` | Use `curl.exe` when following a curl command in PowerShell. The playbook's Windows chat-request examples use `Invoke-RestMethod`. |
| Chat request returns `The model 'unknown' does not exist` | Intermediate · Advanced | The request's `model` value does not match a served model | Get the model ID from `/v1/models` and use that exact ID in the chat request. |
| `torch.OutOfMemoryError` on a GPU with about 95 GiB while loading DeepSeek | Advanced (DGX Station) | The recipe's `--gpus all` let vLLM pick the RTX PRO 6000 instead of the GB300 | Pin the GB300 as in the Advanced tab, Step 3: replace `--gpus all` with `--gpus "device=${GB300_UUID}"`. |
| `engine input registration timed out after 3600s` during FlashInfer autotune | Advanced (DGX Station) | First-run kernel tuning takes longer than the engine-ready timeout | Raise `VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S` (for example `7200`) and mount `~/.cache/vllm` and `~/.cache/flashinfer` so tuning results persist. |
| Memory pressure within capacity | DGX Spark | UMA buffer cache not released | See UMA note below |
| Chat completion returns `content: null` with `finish_reason: length` | Intermediate · Advanced | The request's `max_tokens` was exhausted during reasoning | Increase `max_tokens` in the request and retry. |

## Use another API port

Choose the instructions for the path you are using. Keep the laptop port, DGX host port, and container port distinct; the correct change depends on how the path forwards traffic.

### Intermediate: NVIDIA Sync Custom App

If port 8000 is already in use on your laptop or DGX device, choose a free port, such as 8001:

1. Stop the custom app in Sync by clicking the **x** beside it.
2. Edit the custom app and set **Port** to **8001**.
3. In **Launch Script**, change `PORT=8000` to `PORT=8001`.
4. Save the change and start the app again.
5. In the Intermediate guide's Step 7 URLs, use `http://localhost:8001` instead of `http://localhost:8000`.

All supplied Intermediate scripts use Docker host networking. The `PORT` value sets vLLM's port on the DGX device, and Sync forwards the same port to your laptop. With `PORT=8001`, vLLM listens at `127.0.0.1:8001` on the DGX device.

### Advanced: Host networking, port mapping and SSH tunnel

For a recipe with `--network host`, change the server's `--port 8000` to an unused port, such as `--port 8001`. Use that port for the DGX-local API checks and as the remote port in the SSH tunnel. If you use OpenShell, also update the port in its provider, network policy, and client settings.

If the selected recipe maps DGX host port 8000 and it is already in use, change the host-side port in the recipe's `docker run -p` mapping (the value to the left of the colon) to an unused port, such as 8001. Keep the container-side port and `vllm serve --port` unchanged. Use the new DGX host port for the device-local API checks and as `<dgx-host-port>` in the SSH tunnel command. Use the selected `<laptop-port>` in requests sent through the tunnel.

For tunnel-only access, bind the DGX host-side port to `127.0.0.1`; publish it on other network interfaces only with deliberate access controls.

In the Advanced tab's Step 7 tunnel command, the leftmost port is the laptop port and the rightmost port is the DGX host port. If only the laptop port is busy, change the leftmost port and use it in the laptop client's API URL.

> [!NOTE]
> **Unified memory (UMA).** On hardware platforms with unified memory, GPU and CPU share memory dynamically. Some applications have not yet been updated for UMA, so you may hit memory issues even within capacity. If that happens, manually flush the buffer cache:
> ```bash
> sudo sh -c 'sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches'
> ```

> [!NOTE]
> **Monitoring GPU memory with UMA.** Because of unified memory, `nvidia-smi --query-gpu` memory fields report `N/A`. Use plain `nvidia-smi` instead.
